passage: In Lindiwe's class in Durban, Ms Noa liked riddles. On Friday she said, "Here's a man. He's quiet, wears glasses, and loves reading books. Is he more likely a librarian or a farmer?" Lindiwe's hand shot up. "Librarian! Obviously." Most of the class agreed. Ms Noa smiled and drew on the board. "In our whole province, how many libraries are there? Not many. And how many farms?" The children called out guesses. "Lots! Thousands!" "And do some farmers love reading?" Lindiwe thought of her own uncle, who farmed sugarcane and read every night by lamp. "Yes." "So if there are far more farmers, and some of them are quiet book lovers..." Lindiwe frowned. "Then he's probably a farmer." She felt a bit cheated, and a bit clever.

qa.q: What did Lindiwe first guess the quiet man was?
qa.a: Librarian.

qa.q: Why did "librarian" feel so obvious to Lindiwe?
qa.a: The description matched her picture of a librarian so well that she felt excited and confident, without thinking about how many more farmers there are.

qa.q: How did Ms Noa help the class think better?
qa.a: She asked how many libraries and farms there are, so the children started from how common each job is before looking at the description.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe's uncle show the other side of the riddle?
qa.a: He farms sugarcane and reads every night, showing that many farmers can fit the quiet, bookish description too.

grounding: Shows a child guessing a quiet book lover must be a librarian, forgetting there are far more farmers, until a teacher brings in the numbers.

passage: In the school library period in Nashik, Nirmala ma'am played a guessing game. "A man keeps his desk very tidy, wears a pressed shirt, and loves numbers. Is he a bank manager or a farmer?" Kishore jumped up. "Bank manager!" Nirmala ma'am nodded slowly. "How many bank managers are in our taluka?" Kishore thought. "Maybe... five? Six?" "And how many farmers?" "Everyone's father! Thousands." "Could a farmer be tidy and love numbers?" Kishore thought of his neighbour, who kept every rainfall and price in a fat notebook and ironed his shirt for market day. "Yes." "So which is more likely?" Kishore sat down slowly. "Farmer. Because there are so many more." He felt annoyed and pleased at the same time.

qa.q: How many bank managers did Kishore guess were in the taluka?
qa.a: Maybe five or six.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he sat down slowly?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and pleased at the same time, surprised that the numbers beat the description he had been so sure about.

qa.q: What could Kishore ask himself next time he guesses someone's job?
qa.a: How common each job is around him first, and then whether the description really fits only one of them.

qa.q: How might Nirmala ma'am see Kishore's quick answer?
qa.a: She probably sees it as a natural mistake and uses his neighbour's example to let him find the better answer himself.

grounding: Shows a child guessing a tidy, number-loving man must be a bank manager, forgetting how many more farmers there are.

passage:
Monday. A new man moved into the flat below Madhav's. He wore thick glasses and carried a stack of books up the stairs. "He's a professor," Madhav told his friend Ojas. "Definitely."
Wednesday. Ojas's mother, who knew everyone in the building, laughed when she heard. "Professors? There are maybe two in this whole area. Shopkeepers, drivers, clerks, hundreds." "But the books!" Madhav said. "Lots of people read," she said.
Saturday. At the vegetable market, Madhav saw the man behind a stall of tomatoes and onions, reading between customers. He sold them half a kilo of onions and asked Madhav what he was reading in school. Madhav walked home thinking. The books had made him forget how few professors there were, and how many stall owners.

qa.q: What did the new man carry up the stairs?
qa.a: A stack of books.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he saw the man at the vegetable stall?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a bit silly, seeing that the books had made him forget how few professors there were.

qa.q: What does Ojas's mother's advice suggest Madhav try next time?
qa.a: To think about how many people in the area do each job before guessing from one detail like books.

qa.q: How might the stall owner feel if he knew Madhav's guess?
qa.a: He might be amused or flattered, and perhaps a little tired that reading is linked only to professors.

grounding: Shows over several days a child guessing a bookish neighbour must be a professor, forgetting how common other jobs are.

passage:
Dear Gurleen,
You won't believe what happened this week. On Monday someone posted a photo in our colony group: a leopard near Block C, at night. The photo was blurry, but the man who posted it is a retired army officer, very serious, so everyone believed him. So did I. I stopped walking to tuition alone, and I made Mummy drive me.
On Thursday Papa asked, "How often do leopards come into a city colony?" I said, well, it happens. He showed me that in thirty years, there had been no leopard anywhere in our district. "And big stray dogs?" Every night.
On Friday the forest department checked the camera near Block C. It was the fat yellow dog from the dhaba.
I'm walking again. And I'm embarrassed.
Raghav

qa.q: Who posted the leopard photo in the colony group?
qa.a: A retired army officer, very serious.

qa.q: Why did Raghav believe the leopard story?
qa.a: Raghav felt scared and trusted it because a serious retired officer posted it, forgetting how rare leopards in a city colony are.

qa.q: What question from Papa helped, and why?
qa.a: "How often do leopards come into a city colony?" It made Raghav start from how rare the event is before trusting a blurry report.

qa.q: How might the retired officer feel after the camera check?
qa.a: He might feel embarrassed, having frightened the colony with a blurry photo of a stray dog.

grounding: A teenager's letter shows Raghav believing a rare leopard sighting because the report seemed reliable, ignoring how uncommon it is.

passage: Chaitanya, you remember the physics paper panic? Let me tell you from my side. So, I'm Farhan, and on Sunday night a senior, a topper, very sure of himself, told me the board paper had leaked. He even said which questions. I believed him completely. He's never wrong about exams. I spent the whole night studying only those five questions. But think about it. How many times in, like, twenty years has our state board paper actually leaked? Once, maybe? And how many times do rumours like this go around? Every single exam. The topper just sounded reliable. I forgot how rare a real leak is. In the morning, none of those questions came. Not one. I had skipped two whole chapters for a rumour. My father said, "Next time, ask how often it's really true."

qa.q: How many questions did the senior say had leaked?
qa.a: Five questions.

qa.q: Why did Farhan believe the senior completely?
qa.a: Farhan felt trusting and anxious, because the senior was a topper who sounded sure, so the rare event of a real leak seemed likely.

qa.q: What does Farhan's father suggest, and why is it good advice?
qa.a: To ask how often such a thing is really true, since real leaks are very rare while rumours come every exam.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya remember the physics paper panic?
qa.a: Chaitanya may remember the stress of that night too, and see Farhan's mistake as common among students.

grounding: A teenager explains believing a rumoured exam leak because a topper sounded reliable, ignoring how rare real leaks are.

passage:
Tuesday. A red warning flashed on Devika's phone: "Your device is infected! 3 viruses found. Call this number now." It had an official-looking shield and her phone company's colours. Devika's heart pounded. "My phone's been hacked," she told Zeenat at lunch. "Look, it even knows my phone model."
Wednesday. Devika hadn't called the number, but she was scared to use her phone. Zeenat asked her brother, who worked in IT. He said real hacks of ordinary phones like hers were rare, and fake warnings like this were everywhere, every day.
Thursday. Devika showed the screen to her father. He closed the browser, and the warning disappeared. He showed her how to block pop-ups. "It looked so real," Devika said. "That's the point," he said. "The trick is common. The hack isn't."

qa.q: What did the red warning on Devika's phone say?
qa.a: Your device is infected! 3 viruses found. Call this number now.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when the warning flashed?
qa.a: She felt frightened, heart pounding, sure her phone had been hacked because the warning looked official.

qa.q: What helped Devika, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: Asking Zeenat's brother and then her father, who explained fake warnings are common; next time she can remember how rare real hacks are before panicking.

qa.q: How does Devika's father see the warning?
qa.a: He sees it as a common trick, which is why he closes it calmly and teaches her to block pop-ups.

grounding: Shows a teenager sure her phone was hacked because a warning looked reliable, ignoring how rare real hacks are and how common fakes are.

passage: The college health camp result came on Friday evening, and the lab was closed until Monday. Chandrika read the message three times: "Screening test for a rare blood condition: POSITIVE. Please consult your doctor." Her hands went cold. She searched online. The condition was serious. By midnight she had read about it for four hours and was crying on the hostel floor. Her roommate Lakshmi sat beside her. "What does it say about how many positives turn out to be real?" Chandrika hadn't looked. Lakshmi found the lab's own leaflet. The condition was very rare, and the screening test was meant to catch everyone who might have it, so most people who tested positive turned out to be fine on the second test. Chandrika slept badly, but she slept. On Monday the doctor ordered the confirmation test. It came back clear.

qa.q: When would the lab open after Chandrika got the result?
qa.a: Until Monday, since the lab was closed.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling on Friday night?
qa.a: She felt terrified and overwhelmed, crying on the hostel floor after hours of reading about a serious condition.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi's question help Chandrika see, and what was the wise next step?
qa.a: That for a very rare condition most positive screenings turn out fine; the wise step was waiting for the doctor's confirmation test, not the internet.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt sitting with Chandrika at midnight?
qa.a: Lakshmi was probably worried for her friend but calm, wanting to help her look at the facts instead of the fear.

grounding: Shows a student panicking over a positive screening for a rare condition, not realising most such positives are false alarms, until the facts and a doctor step in.

passage: In their Pune flat, Payal stared at the report from the company health check. One line was flagged in red: a screening test for a rare liver condition, "reactive." She stopped eating. She told her sister Tanuja she was sure she had it. "The report says so." Tanuja, who worked at a diagnostic lab, sat down with her. "Payal, how rare is this condition?" "Very rare. It says so here." "Right. So when thousands of healthy people take a screening test, a few will show up reactive even though they're fine. For something this rare, those false alarms can be more than the real cases." Payal blinked. "So I probably don't have it?" "Probably not. But we don't guess. The doctor will order the proper test." Payal went to the doctor the next morning. The second test was normal. She cried with relief in the car.

qa.q: What was flagged in red on Payal's report?
qa.a: A screening test for a rare liver condition, "reactive."

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she stopped eating?
qa.a: She felt frightened and certain she had the rare condition because the report seemed to say so.

qa.q: How did Tanuja help Payal, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She explained that false alarms can outnumber real cases for rare conditions, and still insisted on seeing the doctor for the proper test.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel watching her sister's fear?
qa.a: Tanuja probably felt concerned but steady, using her lab knowledge to calm Payal without dismissing her.

grounding: Shows a young adult sure she has a rare condition after a positive screening, until her sister explains false alarms and a doctor checks.

passage: I sat next to Nitin in the security team when the alert came in: the system had flagged Maria from accounts as a possible insider threat. Two managers wanted her suspended at once. Nitin didn't move. He asked, "How many people here have ever actually been insiders?" Out of eight hundred staff, in five years: none. "And how many alerts has this system sent?" Forty-two. All false. So he started from that: real cases almost never happen here. Then he looked at the specific evidence. Maria had downloaded a big file at night. That raised the chance a little. So he called the IT security consultant and asked her to explain what exactly the alert measured. It turned out Maria had been working from home before the audit. Nitin closed the alert. The managers went quiet. I remember Maria never even knew.

qa.q: How many alerts had the system sent in five years?
qa.a: Forty-two. All false.

qa.q: Why did Nitin not move when the managers wanted Maria suspended?
qa.a: He seemed calm and careful, wanting to start from how rare real insider cases are before reacting to the alert.

qa.q: What made Nitin's approach sound?
qa.a: He began with the base rate, adjusted for the specific evidence, and asked the security consultant to explain the alert before deciding.

qa.q: How might Maria have been affected if the managers had acted at once?
qa.a: She could have been suspended and shamed for simply working from home before the audit.

grounding: An observer describes a careful analyst starting from how rare insider cases are, adjusting for evidence, and asking an expert to explain an alert.

passage:
Tuesday. The nurse at the maternity hospital said Parveen's newborn had not passed the first hearing screen in one ear. Parveen's heart dropped. Her sister Aparna began searching online. Parveen stopped her. "Before we read anything, let's ask how common it really is."
Thursday. At the follow-up, Parveen asked the audiologist directly: "Out of all babies who don't pass this first screen, how many truly have a hearing problem?" The audiologist explained that most don't; fluid in the ear after birth is common and often clears. Parveen let herself breathe, but she still asked what signs to watch for and when the retest would be.
The next Friday. The retest was clear in both ears. Aparna hugged her. "You were so calm." "I wasn't calm," Parveen said. "I just started from the odds."

qa.q: What did the nurse say on Tuesday?
qa.a: That Parveen's newborn had not passed the first hearing screen in one ear.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling on Tuesday, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: Her heart dropped with fear, but she stopped herself from searching and chose to ask how common a real problem was first.

qa.q: What made Parveen's approach wise?
qa.a: She asked the audiologist how often a failed first screen means a real problem, then still asked about signs and the retest, combining the odds with professional advice.

qa.q: How might Aparna have seen Parveen during those days?
qa.a: Aparna saw her as calm, though Parveen was actually frightened and managing it by starting from the odds.

grounding: Shows a young mother starting with how common a real problem is after a failed screen, then asking a professional to explain before fearing the worst.

passage: Yamini, you asked why I always ask "how often?" first. Let your Yusuf Nana tell you. When I was your age, a young engineer on the Kota bridge maintenance team, a new sensor sent an alarm: possible crack in the third pier. My seniors wanted the bridge closed that same day. Thousands of trucks, a whole city stuck. I was scared, but I asked the sensor supplier one question: "How often has a real crack shown up on bridges like this?" Rarely, they said, maybe once in many years. "And false alarms?" Weekly, in the monsoon, from water in the joints. So I started there. Then I looked for other evidence: no new sag, no cracks in the paint. I asked the senior structural expert to check by hand before we decided. She found water in the sensor box. The bridge stayed open, and we fixed the sensor.

qa.q: Which pier did the sensor flag?
qa.a: The third pier.

qa.q: What was young Yusuf feeling when the alarm came?
qa.a: He felt scared, knowing both a real crack and a needless closure would be serious.

qa.q: Which choice in the story led to the right decision?
qa.a: Asking how often real cracks and false alarms happened, checking other evidence, and having the senior expert inspect by hand before closing the bridge.

qa.q: How might the seniors who wanted the bridge closed see the result?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and maybe a little embarrassed, since the sensor box only had water in it.

grounding: An elder recalls starting from how rare real cracks were, adjusting for other evidence, and asking an expert to check a sensor alarm.

passage: When Disha joined our class in Class 10, she hardly spoke. She drew in the margins of her notebook and wore a scarf with little moons on it. I'm Ujjwal, and I decided at once that she was a shy artist who wrote secret poems at night and probably wanted to live in the mountains. It felt so true. More true, somehow, than just "she likes drawing." In the psychology club, our teacher gave us a quiz with exactly this: which is likelier for a quiet girl, being an artist, or being an artist who writes poems? Most of us picked the second. The teacher smiled. "Every poet-artist is also an artist. So 'artist' can't be less likely." I felt a bit stupid. Later I asked Disha. She liked drawing. She hated poetry.

qa.q: What did the teacher's point help Ujjwal see, and what could Ujjwal do next time?
qa.a: That every poet-artist is also an artist, so the simpler story is always at least as likely; next time Ujjwal could ask the person instead of adding details.

qa.q: How might Disha feel about the story Ujjwal made up about her?
qa.a: Disha might find it odd or a little funny, since she likes drawing but hates poetry.

grounding: A teenager looks back on believing a quiet classmate was a shy artist who wrote poems, more likely than just an artist, because details made it feel truer.

passage:
Class 11 psychology, teacher's note, 14 November.
Today I gave the class a short story: "Meenal is quiet, wears paint-stained jeans, and spends breaks alone." Then two options. A: Meenal is an artist. B: Meenal is an artist who writes poetry and plans to live in a hill town. Keerthana, one of my sharpest students, picked B at once. "It just fits better," she said. Twenty-two of thirty-one students agreed with her.
I drew two circles on the board, "artists," and inside it a small one, "artists who write poetry and want hill towns." Keerthana stared. "B is inside A. It can't be more likely." She laughed, a little embarrassed.
Next class: I'll show them how adding details to rumours works the same way.

qa.q: How many of the thirty-one students agreed with Keerthana?
qa.a: Twenty-two of thirty-one students.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana laugh when she saw the circles?
qa.a: She felt a little embarrassed, seeing that the detailed option she found so fitting was inside the simpler one and couldn't be more likely.

qa.q: How did the teacher help the class, and why does the picture work?
qa.a: By drawing the small circle inside the big one, which shows that every extra detail makes a story narrower and less likely.

qa.q: How might Meenal, if she were real, feel about option B?
qa.a: She might feel boxed in by a detailed story that goes far beyond anything anyone knew about her.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager choosing a detailed story as more likely than a simpler one, because details make it feel truer.

passage: In Karnal, Simran had been planning the college cultural fest for two weeks. Her plan was beautiful: the MLA would inaugurate it, a famous folk singer from Chandigarh would perform for free, the local sweet shop would sponsor food, three nearby colleges would send teams, and the local TV channel would cover it. passage: In a café in Copenhagen, Lars laid out his startup plan for Ines on a napkin. "We build the app by March. Then a big bike company notices us. Then they partner with us. Then the city puts us on its website. Then we get investors." He drew arrows between every step, grinning. The more he talked, the more real it felt to him. Ines, who studied statistics, didn't laugh. "How likely is each step?" "I don't know. Maybe half?" She did the maths on the napkin. "Half, times half, times half, times half, times half. That's about three in a hundred that all of it happens." Lars stared. "But it sounds so good when I say it all." "That's the trap," Ines said. "Every 'and then' makes it sound better and makes it less likely." He crossed out four arrows and circled the first step.

qa.q: What chance did Ines work out for the whole plan?
qa.a: About three in a hundred that all of it happens.

qa.q: Why did the plan feel more real the more Lars talked?
qa.a: Each vivid step made Lars feel more excited and sure, even though adding steps made the whole plan less likely.

passage:
Planning meeting, 12 March. My notes as project coordinator.
Salma pitched the new rural delivery scheme today. It was the most convincing pitch I've heard all year: drones from the district hub, village volunteers to receive them, a mobile app in three languages, a state subsidy by June, and a partnership with the postal department. The room loved it. People were nodding at every step.
I felt the pull too. Then I noticed: every step depended on the one before. I asked the team, gently, "If each of these five things has a good chance, say seven in ten, what's the chance all five happen?" Someone did it on a phone. Less than two in ten. Salma looked stung, then thoughtful.
Next step: we'll pilot just the volunteer network in one village first. Naveen

qa.q: How many things did Salma's pitch depend on?
qa.a: Five things.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while the room loved the pitch?
qa.a: Naveen felt the pull of it too, then grew uneasy on noticing every step depended on the one before.

qa.q: What did Naveen suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Piloting just the volunteer network in one village first, because a long chain of steps is much less likely to work all together.

qa.q: How did Salma seem to take Naveen's question?
qa.a: Salma looked stung at first, then thoughtful, seeing how the chance dropped with each added step.

grounding: A coordinator's note shows noticing that a persuasive, detailed pitch depends on many steps and reminding the team that each extra step lowers the chance of success.

passage:
Wednesday night.
Francis gave the pitch today for the new customer-loyalty plan. It was brilliant, honestly. Personal messages, a points app, a partnership with the gym next door, a TV ad, and a festival launch. By the end, half the room was clapping.
I clapped too. But on the train home I kept thinking. Every single thing had to work. The app on time. The gym saying yes. The TV slot. The festival date. If any one failed, the story fell apart. The more detailed it got, the more believable it felt, and the less likely it was.
Tomorrow I'll ask Francis, kindly, if we can list each step with a rough chance next to it. And maybe start with the one part that doesn't depend on anyone else, the personal messages.
Thomas
